rv.q: Julie is preparing to celebrate her eighteenth birthday with a party to which she's invited "not many people—a hundred?" Her father is away, and the vast building is their own. The one floor we see in Loren Elstein's excellent set design is the kitchen, complete with enormous island unit and sleek cupboards.

It's a measure of the remarkable performance of Synnøve Karlsen, in her stage debut, that she pulls it off in a heady mix of constant mood changes, wild dance, serious confessions and never-ending drinking.
Laura Lomas has done an excellent job of creating a unique and contemporary adaptation aimed at a Gen Z audience, highlighting the everyday struggles young adults face in the world of today.

The brilliant idea of the production is to employ as partygoers, between scenes, members of Frantic Assembly's Ignite nationwide talent development programme for 16 to 24-year-olds, providing startlingly acrobatic flashes of dance and movement.

cn.t: Lomas's modern update of Strindberg's Miss Julie earns solid praise for its punchy, contemporary reimagining that successfully translates 18th-century themes to today's world, though critics suggest the connection to the original remains somewhat loose.
